Empirical Research Plan:  “Do pro-business state policies redirect U.S. manufacturing activity?”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Method:  Border‐county Difference-in-Differences (DiD) combined with an event-study.  
Why it fits:

•  Policy variation is discrete at state borders, while geography, climate and transportation networks vary smoothly across those borders ⇒ a spatial discontinuity we can exploit.  
•  Because right-to-work (RTW) laws were adopted at different dates (1944–1986), we can add the time dimension and estimate a dynamic treatment effect.  
•  Using only counties within a narrow band (≤25 miles) of each relevant border makes the treatment and control counties highly comparable, turning the design into an RDD “in space” embedded in a DiD framework (“difference-in-discontinuities”).  
•  County- and border‐pair fixed effects plus year fixed effects absorb all time-invariant local heterogeneity and national shocks.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable
    Treat_it = 1 if county i is in a state that has an RTW law in force in year t; 0 otherwise.

Control group
    Border-neighbor counties (≤25 miles from the same border segment) that are in a non-RTW state in year t.

Treatment timing / event date
    For each treated county i, the event year is the first year its state’s RTW law became effective (e.g., 1944 for FL & AR, 1986 for ID).

Running variable and cutoff
    Distance (in miles) from county centroid to the closest point on the border.  The cutoff is 0 at the border; we symmetrically trim at |distance| ≤ 25.  (We will also test 10- and 50-mile bands.)

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends (conditional)
    Absent the RTW law, manufacturing employment shares of counties on opposite sides of the same border would have evolved similarly.  
    Plausibility: Same labor-market area, roads, climate, resource endowments.  We can check with pre-treatment event-study coefficients.

A2. No interference / spillovers
    The RTW policy in state A should not directly change manufacturing employment in counties just across the border in state B except via relocation.  
    Plausibility: Some cross-border commuting exists, but plant-location decisions (our outcome) are lumpy and mostly immobile; we still test for negative spillovers on the control side.

A3. Exogeneity of adoption timing within border pairs
    The exact year a state enacted RTW is unrelated to unobserved county-level manufacturing shocks within the 25-mile strip.  
    Plausibility: RTW adoption was politically driven and state-wide; local shocks are unlikely to influence statewide votes.  We check by testing for pre-trends and by controlling for state political variables in robustness.

A4. Stable unit definition
    County boundaries and employment measurement are stable over the sample.  The Census uses consistent county FIPS codes over time, so this is largely satisfied.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent pro-business policies (tax cuts, subsidies) adopted alongside RTW  
    •  Mitigation: Control for the Fantus business-climate index in state-year; include state-year fixed effects interacted with region; test whether dropping states that bundle many policies changes results.

T2. Differential long-run demographic trends (e.g., Sunbelt migration, air-conditioning adoption)  
    •  Mitigation: (i) Very narrow border band; (ii) county fixed effects; (iii) allow county-specific linear time trends in robustness; (iv) placebo borders that do NOT separate RTW from non-RTW.

T3. Sorting of firms or workers exactly at passage year (anticipation)  
    •  Mitigation: Include leads of treatment in event-study; insignificant leads imply limited anticipation.  Also re-estimate excluding two years around adoption.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed-effects
library(sunab)       # event-study coding helper (or build manually)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------
cnty <- read_csv("county_data.csv")   # assume file has 1947-1992 panel

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------
cnty <- cnty %>% 
  mutate(manuf_share = manuf_emp / total_emp,
         rtwyear     = state_rtw_year,           # first year RTW law active
         rtw_in_force= if_else(year >= rtwyear, 1, 0, missing = 0),
         abs_dist    = abs(distance_to_border)) %>% 
  filter(abs_dist <= 25)                         # narrow border band

# Create unique border-pair id (e.g., “GA-FL-east”)
# already in data as border_id
cnty <- cnty %>% mutate(border_id = as.factor(border_id))

# 3. Main DiD specification -----------------------------------------
# Manufacturing share on log scale optional
did_mod <- feols(manuf_share ~ rtw_in_force | county + year, 
                 data   = cnty, 
                 cluster= ~border_id)
summary(did_mod)

# 4. Event-study -----------------------------------------------------
cnty <- cnty %>% mutate(event_time = year - rtwyear)

event_mod <- feols(manuf_share ~ sunab(rtwyear, year) | county + year, 
                   data = cnty, cluster = ~border_id)
iplot(event_mod)           # Plot leads/lags

# 5. Robustness: alternate bandwidth (10 miles) ----------------------
cnty10 <- filter(cnty, abs_dist <= 10)
did_10  <- feols(manuf_share ~ rtw_in_force | county + year, 
                 data   = cnty10, cluster = ~border_id)
etable(did_mod, did_10, se = "cluster")

# 6. Placebo: shift adoption year 5 years earlier --------------------
cnty <- cnty %>% mutate(fake_treat = if_else(year >= rtwyear - 5, 1, 0))
placebo <- feols(manuf_share ~ fake_treat | county + year, 
                 data   = cnty, cluster = ~border_id)
summary(placebo)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: Positive—RTW (and associated pro-business package) should raise the manufacturing share on the treated side relative to the control side.

Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope):  
•  Pre-period average manufacturing share in border counties ≈ 20 %.  
•  Literature suggests RTW boosts manufacturing employment 10–20 % in the long run.  
•  Hence I expect a +2 to +4 percentage-point increase in manufacturing share (roughly +0.15 SD) within 10 years of adoption.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No simultaneous shocks at border   1  
C2: Within-border parallel pre-trends   1  
C3: No treatment anticipation/leads zero 1  
C4: Stable composition / no sorting    0.5 (some migration possible)  
C5: Correct functional form & bandwidth  0.5 (multiple bandwidths tested)  

Total ≈ 4/5 – design is fairly strong but still needs careful robustness work.

------------------------------------------------------------
